claim: 270 human bZIP pairs were examined for DNA binding specificities
source: Guided by protein dimerization properties, we examined DNA binding specificities of 270 human bZIP pairs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of bZIP pairs examined in the study.

claim: DNA interactomes of 80 heterodimers and 22 homodimers were revealed
source: DNA interactomes of 80 heterodimers and 22 homodimers revealed that 72% of heterodimer motifs correspond to conjoined half-sites preferred by partnering monomers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly reports the number of heterodimers and homodimers for which DNA interactomes were obtained.

claim: 72% of heterodimer motifs correspond to conjoined half-sites preferred by partnering monomers
source: DNA interactomes of 80 heterodimers and 22 homodimers revealed that 72% of heterodimer motifs correspond to conjoined half-sites preferred by partnering monomers.
evidence: The abstract provides a quantitative result from the DNA interactome analysis.

claim: 12% of heterodimer motifs are composed of variably-spaced half-sites
source: Remarkably, the remaining motifs are composed of variably-spaced half-sites (12%) or 'emergent' sites (16%) that cannot be readily inferred from half-site preferences of partnering monomers.
evidence: The abstract provides a quantitative breakdown of heterodimer motif types.

claim: 16% of heterodimer motifs are 'emergent' sites that cannot be readily inferred from half-site preferences of partnering monomers
source: Remarkably, the remaining motifs are composed of variably-spaced half-sites (12%) or 'emergent' sites (16%) that cannot be readily inferred from half-site preferences of partnering monomers.
evidence: The abstract provides a quantitative breakdown of heterodimer motif types and defines emergent sites.

claim: Binding sites were biochemically validated by EMSA-FRET analysis
source: These binding sites were biochemically validated by EMSA-FRET analysis and validated in vivo by ChIP-seq data from human cell lines.
evidence: The abstract states that EMSA-FRET was used to validate the binding sites identified.

claim: Binding sites were validated in vivo by ChIP-seq data from human cell lines
source: These binding sites were biochemically validated by EMSA-FRET analysis and validated in vivo by ChIP-seq data from human cell lines.
evidence: The abstract states that ChIP-seq data was used for in vivo validation.

claim: Different bZIP partners confer distinct cognate site preferences on ATF3
source: Focusing on ATF3, we observed distinct cognate site preferences conferred by different bZIP partners, and demonstrated that genome-wide binding of ATF3 is best explained by considering many dimers in which it participates.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that ATF3 shows different DNA binding preferences depending on its dimerization partner.

claim: Genome-wide binding of ATF3 is best explained by considering many dimers in which it participates
source: Focusing on ATF3, we observed distinct cognate site preferences conferred by different bZIP partners, and demonstrated that genome-wide binding of ATF3 is best explained by considering many dimers in which it participates.
evidence: The abstract states that multiple ATF3 dimers are needed to explain genome-wide binding patterns.

claim: The compendium of bZIP-DNA interactomes predicted bZIP binding to 156 disease associated SNPs
source: Importantly, our compendium of bZIP-DNA interactomes predicted bZIP binding to 156 disease associated SNPs, of which only 20 were previously annotated with known bZIP motifs.
evidence: The abstract provides a specific number of disease-associated SNPs predicted to affect bZIP binding.

claim: Only 20 of the 156 disease-associated SNPs predicted to affect bZIP binding were previously annotated with known bZIP motifs
source: Importantly, our compendium of bZIP-DNA interactomes predicted bZIP binding to 156 disease associated SNPs, of which only 20 were previously annotated with known bZIP motifs.
evidence: The abstract provides a comparison between newly predicted SNPs and previously annotated ones.

claim: bZIPs bind DNA as either homo- or heterodimers
source: The bZIP class of human TFs is well suited to play a role in signal integration and combinatorial transcriptional control (Lamb and McKnight, 1991; Miller, 2009; Tsukada et al., 2011). bZIPs bind DNA as either homo- or heterodimers
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the dimerization requirement for bZIP DNA binding, supported by citations.

claim: JUN and FOS can bind to DNA as a heterodimer
source: the discovery in 1988 that JUN and FOS could bind to DNA as a heterodimer immediately suggested the potential for combinatorial regulation by this family (Franza et al., 1988; Lamb and McKnight, 1991).
evidence: The introduction cites a historical discovery about JUN-FOS heterodimerization.

claim: The human bZIP network displays greater ability to form heterodimers compared to simpler eukaryotes
source: Interestingly, the human bZIP network displays greater ability to form heterodimers compared to simpler eukaryotes, suggesting that more complex combinatorial regulation may contribute to organismal complexity (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction states a comparative observation about bZIP heterodimerization across species, supported by citation.

claim: More complex combinatorial regulation may contribute to organismal complexity
source: Interestingly, the human bZIP network displays greater ability to form heterodimers compared to simpler eukaryotes, suggesting that more complex combinatorial regulation may contribute to organismal complexity (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction presents a hypothesis about the relationship between combinatorial regulation and organismal complexity.

claim: ATF3 homodimer acts as a repressor
source: For example, ATF3 homodimer acts as a repressor, whereas ATF3•JUN activates transcription (Hsu et al., 1992).
evidence: The introduction states the regulatory function of ATF3 homodimer, supported by citation.

claim: ATF3•JUN activates transcription
source: For example, ATF3 homodimer acts as a repressor, whereas ATF3•JUN activates transcription (Hsu et al., 1992).
evidence: The introduction states the regulatory function of ATF3•JUN heterodimer, supported by citation.

claim: Fifty-three bZIPs are encoded by the human genome
source: Fifty-three bZIPs encoded by the human genome can be grouped into 21 families
evidence: The introduction provides the total number of human bZIP proteins.

claim: Human bZIPs can be grouped into 21 families
source: Fifty-three bZIPs encoded by the human genome can be grouped into 21 families
evidence: The introduction provides the classification of human bZIP proteins.

claim: bZIP homodimers bind at least six distinct classes of DNA motifs
source: and as homodimers they are known to bind at least six distinct classes of DNA motifs, including sites labeled as TRE, CRE, CRE-L, CAAT, PAR, and MARE (Figure 1) (Deppmann et al., 2006; Jolma et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction lists the known DNA motif classes bound by bZIP homodimers, supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: JUN•ATF2 heterodimer binds to a cognate site in the ENK2 promoter that is not bound by either JUN•JUN or ATF2•ATF2 homodimers
source: In 1991, Hai and Curran (1991) showed that some heterodimers have DNA-binding specificities that are distinct from those of each partnering bZIP. For example, JUN•ATF2 heterodimer binds to a cognate site in the ENK2 promoter that is not bound by either JUN•JUN or ATF2•ATF2 homodimers.
evidence: The introduction cites a specific example of heterodimer-specific DNA binding.

claim: 73 of 126 (58%) bZIP pairs that dimerize in the absence of DNA yielded specific cognate sites
source: 73 of 126 (58%) bZIP pairs that dimerize in the absence of DNA yielded specific cognate sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on the success rate of identifying cognate sites for stable dimers, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: 29 of the 144 (20%) bZIP pairs that do not stably associate in the absence of DNA yielded evidence of sequence-specific binding to DNA
source: Surprisingly, 29 of the 144 (20%) bZIP pairs that do not stably associate in the absence of DNA (Kd >1 µM at 21°C) yielded evidence of sequence-specific binding to DNA, indicating that PPIs were stabilized by binding to specific DNA sites (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on DNA-stabilized dimerization, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: PPIs were stabilized by binding to specific DNA sites for bZIP pairs that do not stably associate in the absence of DNA
source: Surprisingly, 29 of the 144 (20%) bZIP pairs that do not stably associate in the absence of DNA (Kd >1 µM at 21°C) yielded evidence of sequence-specific binding to DNA, indicating that PPIs were stabilized by binding to specific DNA sites (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the data on DNA-stabilized dimerization.

claim: Comprehensive DNA-binding specificity is reported for the first time for human ATF2, ATF3, ATF6, ATF6B, CEBPA, CREB1, FOSL1, JUN, MAFB, and NFE2L1
source: Of the 22 homodimers, comprehensive DNA-binding specificity is reported for the first time for human ATF2, ATF3, ATF6, ATF6B, CEBPA, CREB1, FOSL1, JUN, MAFB, and NFE2L1.
evidence: The results section explicitly lists the homodimers for which comprehensive DNA-binding specificity is newly reported.

claim: Several bZIP homodimers (ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3L1, and JUN) enriched more than one motif
source: Notably, several bZIP homodimers (ATF6, ATF6B, CREB3L1, and JUN) enriched more than one motif (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section identifies specific homodimers that bind multiple motifs.

claim: FOS•CEBPG heterodimer prefers the 8 bp conjoined CRE-CAAT site (5'TGACGCAA3')
source: it was surprising to find that closely related heterodimers such as FOS•CEBPG and FOS•CEBPE preferred different arrangements of half-sites, with the former heterodimer preferring the 8 bp conjoined CRE-CAAT site (motif 1 5'TGACGCAA3')
evidence: The results section provides specific DNA sequence preferences for FOS•CEBPG.

claim: FOS•CEBPE heterodimer prefers the 7 bp variably-spaced TRE-CAAT site (5'TGAGCAA3')
source: it was surprising to find that closely related heterodimers such as FOS•CEBPG and FOS•CEBPE preferred different arrangements of half-sites, with the former heterodimer preferring the 8 bp conjoined CRE-CAAT site (motif 1 5'TGACGCAA3') and the latter preferring the 7 bp variably-spaced TRE-CAAT site (motif 4 5'TGAGCAA3').
evidence: The results section provides specific DNA sequence preferences for FOS•CEBPE.

claim: BATF family members switch from a CRE half-site (5′TGAC3′) preferred in homodimers to a CRE-L (5′CCAC3′) half-site preferred by many BATF-containing heterodimers
source: An example of the first category includes a switch in the half-site preferences of BATF family members, from a CRE half-site (5′TGAC3′) that is preferred in homodimers to a CRE-L (5′CCAC3′) half-site that is preferred by many BATF-containing heterodimers
evidence: The results section describes a specific example of emergent site formation through gain-of-specificity.

claim: DDIT3•CEBPG binds to 5′ATTGCA3′ with no apparent requirement for one half-site
source: An example of the second category is DDIT3•CEBPG binding to 5′ATTGCA3′ (motif 5) (Ubeda et al., 1996), with heterodimers displaying no apparent requirement for one half-site.
evidence: The results section describes a specific example of emergent site formation through loss-of-specificity, with citation.

claim: Nine out of the 80 heterodimers (11%) enriched two motifs
source: Nine out of the 80 heterodimers (11%) enriched two motifs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on heterodimers binding multiple motifs.

claim: BATF•CEBPG enriched both CRE-CAAT and CRE-L-CAAT motifs
source: For example, BATF•CEBPG enriched both CRE-CAAT and CRE-L-CAAT motifs.
evidence: The results section provides a specific example of a heterodimer binding two motifs.

claim: CSI intensity correlates with binding affinity
source: The height and color of each point represents the CSI intensity for the corresponding sequence. As noted above, CSI intensity correlates with binding affinity where measured (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Carlson et al., 2010; Hauschild et al., 2009; Puckett et al., 2007; Tietjen et al., 2011; Warren et al., 2006).
evidence: The results section states the correlation between CSI intensity and binding affinity, supported by citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 52 out of 56 bZIP pairs that form stable heterodimers bound the DNA site made by conjoining the half-site preferred by each monomer
source: Consistent with CSI analysis, 52 out of 56 bZIP pairs that form stable heterodimers bound the DNA site made by conjoining the half-site preferred by each monomer.
evidence: The results section provides quantitative EMSA-FRET validation data for conjoined sites.

claim: 6 out of 27 (22%) pairs that do not stably associate in the absence of DNA showed specific binding to conjoined sites
source: Specific binding to conjoined sites was also detected for 6 out of 27 (22%) pairs that do not stably associate in the absence of DNA (PPI: Kd >1 µM at 21°C).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative EMSA-FRET data for DNA-stabilized dimers binding conjoined sites.

claim: ATF3 is initially identified as a suppressor of inflammation and the adaptive immune response in resting cells
source: Activating Transcription Factor 3 (ATF3) is a member of the CREB/ATF family. Initially identified as a suppressor of inflammation and the adaptive immune response in resting cells, ATF3 is now associated with numerous diseases including a variety of aggressive and widely occurring cancers (Tanaka et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: The results section describes the initial characterization of ATF3, supported by citations.

claim: ATF3 is associated with numerous diseases including a variety of aggressive and widely occurring cancers
source: Initially identified as a suppressor of inflammation and the adaptive immune response in resting cells, ATF3 is now associated with numerous diseases including a variety of aggressive and widely occurring cancers (Tanaka et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: The results section states the disease associations of ATF3, supported by citations.

claim: Only 119 genomic sites were common between the four cell lines examined for ATF3 binding
source: Only a small number of sites (119) were common between the four cell lines, although the number increased to 1602 genomic loci if only the ENCODE cells lines (H1, K562, and HEPG2) were examined (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on ATF3 ChIP-seq peak overlap across cell lines, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: 1602 genomic loci were occupied by ATF3 in all three ENCODE cell lines (H1, K562, and HEPG2)
source: Only a small number of sites (119) were common between the four cell lines, although the number increased to 1602 genomic loci if only the ENCODE cells lines (H1, K562, and HEPG2) were examined (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on ATF3 ChIP-seq peak overlap in ENCODE cell lines, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: ATF3 homodimer yielded 0.67–0.77 AUC values for explaining ChIP-seq peaks
source: ATF3 homodimer sites spanning the entire spectrum of CSI intensities (z-scores) yielded 0.67–0.77 AUC values (Supplementary file 1E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative AUC-ROC values for ATF3 homodimer prediction of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: JUN•ATF3 gives 0.85 AUC in the Glioblastoma line
source: For example, JUN•ATF3 gives 0.85 AUC in the Glioblastoma line, whereas BATF3•ATF3 better explains the ChIP-seq peaks in H1 and HepG2 cells with AUC of 0.69 and 0.70, respectively.
evidence: The results section provides specific AUC values for JUN•ATF3 in the Glioblastoma cell line.

claim: BATF3•ATF3 explains ChIP-seq peaks in H1 and HepG2 cells with AUC of 0.69 and 0.70, respectively
source: For example, JUN•ATF3 gives 0.85 AUC in the Glioblastoma line, whereas BATF3•ATF3 better explains the ChIP-seq peaks in H1 and HepG2 cells with AUC of 0.69 and 0.70, respectively.
evidence: The results section provides specific AUC values for BATF3•ATF3 in H1 and HepG2 cell lines.

claim: At an FPR-cutoff of 0.10 in the Glioblastoma cell line, the ATF3 homodimer classified just 39% of the ATF3 ChIP-seq peaks as positive
source: For example, at an FPR-cutoff of 0.10, in the Glioblastoma cell line, the ATF3 homodimer classified just 39% of the ATF3 ChIP-seq peaks as positive, whereas 85% of the peaks are classified positive by at least one of the ATF3-containing dimers at FPR 0.10.
evidence: The results section provides quantitative comparison of homodimer vs. heterodimer performance in explaining ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 85% of ATF3 ChIP-seq peaks in Glioblastoma are classified positive by at least one of the ATF3-containing dimers at FPR 0.10
source: For example, at an FPR-cutoff of 0.10, in the Glioblastoma cell line, the ATF3 homodimer classified just 39% of the ATF3 ChIP-seq peaks as positive, whereas 85% of the peaks are classified positive by at least one of the ATF3-containing dimers at FPR 0.10.
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data showing improved peak classification when considering multiple ATF3 heterodimers.

claim: De novo motif discovery in the blue cluster revealed enrichment of a CRE-CAAT motif
source: In the blue cluster, de novo motif discovery revealed enrichment of a CRE-CAAT motif, which is the motif with maximal CSI intensities for CEBP•ATF3 dimers.
evidence: The results section reports de novo motif discovery results for a specific cluster of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: De novo motif search of ChIP-seq peaks in the green cluster identified the TRE motif
source: De novo motif search of ChIP-seq peaks in the green cluster identified the TRE motif, which is the top ranked motif for ATF3 heterodimers formed with JUNB, JUN, FOS, and FOSL1, all of which are expressed in GBM1 cells (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: The results section reports de novo motif discovery results for another cluster of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: The minor allele of rs10993994 in the promoter of the MSMB gene has been associated with prostate cancer and it creates a cognate site that is bound by CREB1
source: The minor allele of rs10993994 in the promoter of the MSMB gene has been associated with prostate cancer and it creates a cognate site that is bound by CREB1 (Lou et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section describes a known SNP that affects CREB1 binding, supported by citation.

claim: The minor allele of rs12740374 has been associated with myocardial infarction, aberrant plasma levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and enhanced expression of SORT1 gene in the liver
source: Similarly, the minor allele of rs12740374 has been associated with myocardial infarction, aberrant plasma levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and enhanced expression of SORT1 gene in the liver (Musunuru et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section describes a known SNP with multiple disease associations, supported by citation.

claim: The G-to-T change in rs12740374 generates an optimal CAAT site that is bound by CEBPA
source: Biochemical studies have demonstrated that the G-to-T change generates an optimal CAAT site that is bound by CEBPA.
evidence: The results section describes the molecular mechanism by which rs12740374 affects CEBPA binding.

claim: rs7631605 is associated to Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and elevated levels of phosphorylated Tau-181P
source: This allele is associated to Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and elevated levels of phosphorylated Tau-181P (Han et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section describes disease associations for rs7631605, supported by citation.

claim: CSI-Genomescape predicts disruption of the emergent site 5′TGACGCAT3′ by rs7631605
source: The CSI-Genomescape for rs7631605 site is particularly interesting because it predicts disruption of the emergent site 5′TGACGCAT3′ (Figure 7A middle panel).
evidence: The results section describes a prediction for how rs7631605 affects bZIP binding, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: rs1869901 is a variant associated with schizophrenia
source: Additionally, CSI-Genomescape predicts that rs1869901, a variant associated with schizophrenia, impacts binding of FOS•CEBPE by altering a TRE-CAAT site (Figure 7A bottom panel).
evidence: The results section describes the disease association and predicted binding impact of rs1869901, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: rs3758354 is a SNP associated with schizophrenia, depression, and bipolar disorder
source: However, a striking example of predicted increase in binding is rs3758354, a SNP associated with schizophrenia, depression, and bipolar disorder (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section describes disease associations for rs3758354, supported by citation.

claim: rs17293632 is a variant linked to Crohn's autoimmune disorder
source: In contrast, a decrease in FOS•JUN heterodimer binding is predicted for rs17293632, a variant linked to Crohn's autoimmune disorder (Franke et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section describes the disease association for rs17293632, supported by citation.

claim: A total of 156 SNPs yielded a greater than twofold difference in CSI intensity between the reference and alternate alleles
source: A total of 156 SNPs yielded a greater than twofold difference in CSI intensity between the reference and alternate alleles (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on SNPs predicted to affect bZIP binding, with reference to Figure 7C-D.

claim: 80% of the identified changes in SNP binding impact bZIP heterodimers
source: We also report that 80% of the identified changes impact bZIP heterodimers.
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on the proportion of SNP effects on heterodimers vs. homodimers.

claim: Only 20 of 156 SNPs are currently annotated with a bZIP motif in the RegulomeDB database
source: In the richly annotated RegulomeDB database that ties SNP impact to occurrence of TF-binding sites, only 20 of 156 SNPs are currently annotated with a bZIP motif (Boyle et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section compares the newly identified SNPs with existing annotations in RegulomeDB, supported by citation.

claim: 36 human bZIP monomers can form nearly 217 heterodimers
source: Comprehensive PPI analysis has shown that 36 human bZIP monomers can form nearly 217 heterodimers, greatly expanding the repertoire of factors that can potentially bind DNA (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion cites quantitative data on the number of possible bZIP heterodimers.

claim: Nearly 20% of the non-interacting bZIP pairs examined can be induced to dimerize at cognate DNA sites
source: We demonstrate that this diversity of dimers expands the DNA sequence space that can be targeted by bZIPs. Our study further reveals that nearly 20% of the non-interacting bZIP pairs examined can be induced to dimerize at cognate DNA sites, providing yet greater diversity from a modest number of contributing monomers.
evidence: The discussion summarizes a key finding about DNA-induced dimerization.

claim: The DNA-binding profiles for 80 heterodimers and 22 homodimers is the largest bZIP heterodimer DNA-binding data reported to date
source: The DNA-binding profiles for 80 heterodimers, which we report alongside equivalent data for 22 homodimers, is the largest bZIP heterodimer DNA-binding data reported to date and provides unprecedented insight into the impact of heterodimer formation.
evidence: The discussion claims this is the largest dataset of its kind.

claim: Conjoined half-sites were the most abundant class of heterodimer binding sites, with nearly 72% of all heterodimers displaying some affinity for such sites
source: Of the three classes, conjoined half-sites were the most abundant, with nearly 72% of all heterodimers displaying some affinity for such sites.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the quantitative breakdown of heterodimer binding site classes.

claim: The final class of heterodimer binding sites, comprising 16% of the sites, was the 'emergent' class
source: The final class, comprising 16% of the sites, was the least expected 'emergent' class of binding sites, where new non-obvious preferences for half-sites were revealed.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the quantitative breakdown of heterodimer binding site classes.

claim: The ability of ATF3•CEBPB to bind a cognate site within seemingly closed chromatin is consistent with the ability of bZIPs such as CEBPB and FOS•JUN to function as 'pioneer' factors
source: In this context, the ability of ATF3•CEBPB to bind a cognate site within seemingly closed chromatin is consistent with the ability of bZIPs such as CEBPB and FOS•JUN to function as 'pioneer' factors that first associate with closed chromatin and enable binding of additional TFs to yield transcriptionally active euchromatin (Biddie et al., 2011; Garber et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion connects the observed binding to closed chromatin with the known pioneer factor function of certain bZIPs, supported by citations.

claim: Nearly 77% of the 156 SNPs predicted to impact bZIP binding were mapped to bZIP heterodimers
source: Of the 156 SNPs predicted by our CSI profiles to impact bZIP binding, nearly 77% were mapped to bZIP heterodimers, highlighting the importance of determining protein-DNA interactomes for heterodimer TFs.
evidence: The discussion provides quantitative data on the proportion of SNPs affecting heterodimers.

claim: Nearly 64% of the 156 SNPs created bZIP binding sites and were 'gain of function' changes relative to the human reference genome
source: Nearly 64% created bZIP binding sites and were 'gain of function' changes relative to the human reference genome.
evidence: The discussion provides quantitative data on the proportion of SNPs that create vs. disrupt binding sites.

claim: The 270 bZIP pairs examined represent a wide survey of the 666 potential pairs that can be formed by 36 monomers
source: Guided by PPI data, we examined the DNA-binding specificities of 126 stable dimers and 144 bZIP dimers that display no dimerization even at 1 µM. These 270 bZIP pairs represent a wide survey of the 666 potential pairs that can be formed by 36 monomers.
evidence: The discussion contextualizes the scope of the study relative to all possible bZIP pairs.

claim: The average Pearson's correlation for eight replicate samples was 0.8 ± 0.1
source: Repeated experiments demonstrated an average Pearson's correlation r = 0.8 ± 0.1 between CSI intensities from replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative reproducibility data for the SELEX-seq experiments, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reciprocal biotinylation experiments showed Pearson's correlation r = 0.89–0.98
source: In three cases, reciprocal biotinylation of each partner was performed to ensure that the choice of partner did not skew the results (Pearson's correlation for comparing experiments was r = 0.89–0.98; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on the reproducibility of reciprocal experiments, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The DNA specificity of the isolated DNA binding domain (DBD) is typically indistinguishable from the full-length factor for most TFs, including the bZIP class
source: For most TFs, including the bZIP class, the DNA specificity of the isolated DNA binding domain (DBD) is typically indistinguishable from the full-length factor (Jolma et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section justifies the use of bZIP domains rather than full-length proteins, supported by citation.

claim: The previously reported DNA specificity of ATF4 has a higher correlation with the specificity of ATF4•CEBPG heterodimer than with the specificity of the ATF4 homodimer
source: Interestingly, we found that the previously reported DNA specificity of ATF4 has a higher correlation with the specificity of ATF4•CEBPG heterodimer identified in this report than with the specificity of the ATF4 homodimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that CEBPG possibly formed a complex with ATF4 in the cell lysates used in the prior study (Jolma et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section compares current data with previous studies and provides an interpretation, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and citation.

claim: 30 out of the 36 bZIP proteins tested enriched specific DNA sequences as part of at least one dimer
source: Overall, 30 out of the 36 bZIP proteins tested in this study enriched specific DNA sequences as part of at least one dimer.
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on the success rate of identifying DNA binding for the tested bZIPs.

claim: bZIPs that are not known to bind DNA as homodimers did not yield cognate sites (e.g. JUNB and FOS)
source: bZIPs that are not known to bind DNA as homodimers did not yield cognate sites in our studies (e.g. JUNB and FOS) (Deng and Karin, 1993; Hai and Curran, 1991).
evidence: The results section reports negative results for certain bZIPs, supported by citations.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the 102 bZIP-DNA interactomes readily identified six previously known classes of bZIP-binding sites (TRE, CAAT, PAR, MARE, CRE, and CRE-L)
source: Hierarchical clustering of the 102 bZIP-DNA interactomes readily identified six previously known classes of bZIP-binding sites (TRE, CAAT, PAR, MARE, CRE, and CRE-L) (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The results section describes the clustering analysis results, with reference to Figure 1B-C.

claim: Several heterodimers that bind classic bZIP homodimer motifs displayed clear differences in their preference for a subset of sequences categorized under a single consensus motif
source: Interestingly, several heterodimers that bind classic bZIP homodimer motifs such as TRE, CRE-L, or CRE displayed clear differences in their preference for a subset of sequences categorized under a single consensus motif (e.g. compare motifs 9 and 10 in Figure 1 with the CRE-L site).
evidence: The results section describes sub-structure within consensus motifs, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Different homodimers display differences in DNA-binding specificity for sequences categorized under a single consensus motif
source: This was also true for different homodimers (e.g. compare CRE-L binding profiles for ATF6, CREB3, CREB3L1, and XBP1 in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section describes sub-structure within consensus motifs for homodimers.

claim: The second class of heterodimer binding sites contained variably-spaced half-sites, often overlapping by a single nucleotide
source: The second class contained variably-spaced half-sites, often overlapping by a single nucleotide.
evidence: The results section describes the characteristics of variably-spaced heterodimer binding sites.

claim: Emergent sites fall into 'loss of specificity' or 'gain of specificity' categories
source: Emergent sites targeted by heterodimers fall into 'loss of specificity' or 'gain of specificity' categories, as defined above.
evidence: The results section categorizes emergent sites into two types.

claim: In some instances, homodimers bound with low affinity to sites that emerged as high-affinity sites in the context of a heterodimer
source: In some instances, homodimers bound with low affinity to sites that emerged as high-affinity sites in the context of a heterodimer, whereas in other cases entirely new site preferences emerged.
evidence: The results section describes different mechanisms by which emergent sites arise.

claim: In other cases, entirely new site preferences emerged for heterodimers
source: In some instances, homodimers bound with low affinity to sites that emerged as high-affinity sites in the context of a heterodimer, whereas in other cases entirely new site preferences emerged.
evidence: The results section describes different mechanisms by which emergent sites arise.

claim: The preference for one arrangement of half-sites over the other was not amenable to predictions based on the binding preferences of each contributing partner of the heterodimer
source: Similarly, other heterodimers bound both conjoined and variably spaced motifs (see JUNB•ATF3 and MAFB•ATF5 in Supplementary file 2); however, the preference for one arrangement over the other was not amenable to predictions based on the binding preferences of each contributing partner of the heterodimer.
evidence: The results section highlights the unpredictability of heterodimer binding preferences.

claim: Emergent cognate sites pose a particular challenge for current models of DNA binding site predictions that are based on protein homology
source: Emergent sites pose a particular challenge for current models of DNA binding site predictions that are based on protein homology (Weirauch et al., 2014).
evidence: The results section discusses the implications of emergent sites for prediction models, supported by citation.

claim: The 1-mismatch ring of the ATF4•CEBPG SEL indicates that both half-sites are not equally tolerant of mismatches
source: The 1-mismatch ring indicates that both half-sites are not equally tolerant of mismatches, with mismatches in the 5′TGA3′ core of the CRE site dramatically reducing binding, whereas the 5′CAA3′ site is tolerant of deviations at the first position of the half-site but sensitive to deviations in the 5′AA3′ positions.
evidence: The results section describes detailed binding preferences revealed by SEL analysis.

claim: Mismatches in the 5′TGA3′ core of the CRE site dramatically reduce binding by ATF4•CEBPG
source: The 1-mismatch ring indicates that both half-sites are not equally tolerant of mismatches, with mismatches in the 5′TGA3′ core of the CRE site dramatically reducing binding, whereas the 5′CAA3′ site is tolerant of deviations at the first position of the half-site but sensitive to deviations in the 5′AA3′ positions.
evidence: The results section describes specific sequence requirements for ATF4•CEBPG binding.

claim: The 5′CAA3′ site is tolerant of deviations at the first position of the half-site but sensitive to deviations in the 5′AA3′ positions for ATF4•CEBPG binding
source: The 1-mismatch ring indicates that both half-sites are not equally tolerant of mismatches, with mismatches in the 5′TGA3′ core of the CRE site dramatically reducing binding, whereas the 5′CAA3′ site is tolerant of deviations at the first position of the half-site but sensitive to deviations in the 5′AA3′ positions.
evidence: The results section describes specific sequence requirements for ATF4•CEBPG binding.

claim: The emergent site 5'TGACGCAT3' is highly preferred by JUN•ATF3 and to some extent by JUN•CEBPG but not by homodimers formed by ATF3, CEBPG, or JUN
source: An examination of row 3, which displays preferences of all 102 dimers for the emergent site 5'TGACGCAT3', indicates that this site is highly preferred by JUN•ATF3 and to some extent by JUN•CEBPG but not by homodimers formed by ATF3, CEBPG, or JUN (denoted by asterisks).
evidence: The results section describes the specificity of the emergent site for certain heterodimers.

claim: The conjoined CRE-CAAT site is primarily targeted by heterodimers formed by the CEBP family of bZIPs
source: While not as exclusive as the JUN•ATF3 emergent site, the conjoined CRE-CAAT site is primarily targeted by heterodimers formed by the CEBP family of bZIPs.
evidence: The results section describes the binding preferences for the CRE-CAAT site.

claim: The conjoined CRE-CAAT site permits low-affinity binding by the CEBPG homodimer
source: The heatmap does indicate that this heterodimer-preferred site permits low-affinity binding by the CEBPG homodimer.
evidence: The results section notes that homodimers can bind heterodimer-preferred sites with lower affinity.

claim: Substituting 5'CAAT3' with 5'TAAT3' in the CRE-CAAT site perturbs binding by CEBP heterodimers in a non-uniform manner
source: Interestingly, data in row 8 reveals that substituting 5'CAAT3' with 5'TAAT3' in the CRE-CAAT site perturbs binding by CEBP heterodimers in a non-uniform manner, unmasking hidden differential sequence preferences of related heterodimers that are opaque to current models that use protein homology to predict cognate site preferences.
evidence: The results section describes how a single nucleotide change reveals differential binding preferences.

claim: The C-to-T substitution in the CRE-CAAT site expands the repertoire of bZIPs that bind this modified site
source: The C-to-T substitution also expands the repertoire of bZIPs that bind this mutated site. DBP, HLF, and NFIL3 as homo- and hetero- dimers display an unmistakable affinity for this modified CRE-CAAT site that recreates the PAR half-site that is a target of this set of bZIPs.
evidence: The results section describes how a nucleotide substitution creates binding sites for additional bZIPs.

claim: DBP, HLF, and NFIL3 as homo- and hetero-dimers display affinity for the modified CRE-CAAT site with 5'TAAT3' that recreates the PAR half-site
source: DBP, HLF, and NFIL3 as homo- and hetero- dimers display an unmistakable affinity for this modified CRE-CAAT site that recreates the PAR half-site that is a target of this set of bZIPs.
evidence: The results section identifies specific bZIPs that bind the modified site.

claim: A different substitution at the same position (5'GAAT3') dramatically reduces the binding of all bZIPs to this version of the CRE-CAAT site
source: On the other hand, a different substitution at the same position (5'GAAT3') dramatically reduces the binding of all bZIPs to this version of the CRE-CAAT site (row 9).
evidence: The results section describes how a different nucleotide substitution abolishes binding.

claim: For 15 homodimers for which binding to DNA could be detected, the mixed-dye homodimer could be easily distinguished from both of the single-dye homodimers
source: For 15 homodimers for which we could detect binding to DNA, the mixed-dye homodimer could be easily distinguished from both of the single-dye homodimers, as shown for CEBPG and ATF3 homodimers binding to CAAT and CRE sites, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section describes the validation of the EMSA-FRET assay for homodimers, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The ATF3•CEBPG heterodimer bound the conjoined CRE-CAAT site better than either parental homodimer
source: This assay was then used to demonstrate that the ATF3•CEBPG heterodimer bound the conjoined CRE-CAAT site better than either parental homodimer (Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section provides EMSA-FRET validation of heterodimer-specific binding, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Swapping fluorophores did not alter the binding properties of the ATF3•CEBPG heterodimer
source: Furthermore, swapping fluorophores did not alter the binding properties of the resulting heterodimer (last panel of Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section demonstrates that the EMSA-FRET results are not affected by which partner is labeled with which fluorophore, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: DNA fluorescence coincides with the protein FRET signals, confirming that protein-DNA complexes were being observed in the EMSA gels
source: DNA fluorescence coincides with the protein FRET signals, confirming that protein-DNA complexes were being observed in the EMSA gels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section provides validation that the observed signals correspond to protein-DNA complexes, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neither the JUN nor the ATF3 homodimers associate with the emergent site identified for JUN•ATF3
source: The EMSA-FRET data demonstrate clearly that neither the JUN nor the ATF3 homodimers associate with the emergent site identified for JUN•ATF3 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section provides EMSA-FRET validation that the emergent site is heterodimer-specific, with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Emergent sites identified for ATF4•CEBPA and ATF4•JUN were validated by EMSA-FRET as bona fide heterodimer-specific cognate sites
source: Similarly, emergent sites identified for ATF4•CEBPA and ATF4•JUN, and several conjoined sites such as TRE-CAAT for ATF3•CEBPA, CRE-L-CAAT for BATF3•CEBPA, and CRE-CRE-L for BATF3•JUN, were validated by EMSA-FRET as bona fide heterodimer-specific cognate sites that show weaker binding, or no binding, by the contributing homodimers (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section provides EMSA-FRET validation of multiple heterodimer-specific sites, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: EMSA-FRET data validate the ability of BATF3 to bind emergent CRE-L half-sites as a heterodimer
source: EMSA-FRET data also validate the ability of BATF3 to bind emergent CRE-L half-sites as a heterodimer (in addition to the CRE site preferred by the homodimer).
evidence: The results section provides EMSA-FRET validation of emergent half-site preferences for BATF3 heterodimers.

claim: ATF3 is able to interact with a large variety of TFs to function as a regulatory hub of cellular adaptive response
source: ATF3 is able to interact with a large variety of TFs to function as a regulatory hub of cellular adaptive response (Gilchrist et al., 2006; Hai et al., 1999, 2010).
evidence: The results section describes the role of ATF3 as a regulatory hub, supported by citations.

claim: As a homodimer, ATF3 binds to CRE sites and represses a wide array of genes
source: As a homodimer, ATF binds to CRE sites and represses a wide array of genes (Hai et al., 1999, 2010).
evidence: The results section describes the function of ATF3 homodimer, supported by citations.

claim: As a heterodimer with JUN or JUND, ATF3 activates transcription of targeted genes
source: However, as a heterodimer with JUN or JUND, ATF3 activates transcription of targeted genes (Chu et al., 1994; Filén et al., 2010; Hsu et al., 1992).
evidence: The results section describes the function of ATF3 heterodimers, supported by citations.

claim: DNA-binding specificities could be assigned with high confidence to nine ATF3 heterodimers
source: To test the hypothesis that heterodimerization with other bZIPs might alter DNA-binding specificity and possibly genomic targets, we analyzed SELEX-seq for 20 different ATF3 heterodimers spanning the full range of PPI affinities. DNA-binding specificities could be assigned with high confidence to nine heterodimers that displayed a range of DNA sequence preferences, including affinity for the CRE site preferred by the homodimer (Figures 4A and B).
evidence: The results section reports the number of ATF3 heterodimers with confident DNA-binding specificity assignments, with reference to Figures 4A and B.

claim: The motifs enriched by the ATF3 homo- and heterodimers can be described in five broad categories: CRE, TRE, CRE-CAAT, CRE-L, and the emergent 5′TGACGCAT3′ site
source: The motifs enriched by the ATF3 homo- and heterodimers can be described in five broad categories: CRE, TRE, CRE-CAAT, CRE-L, and the emergent 5′TGACGCAT3′ site (Figure 4B).
evidence: The results section categorizes the motifs bound by ATF3 dimers, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: CRE-CAAT sites are preferably bound by ATF3•CEBPG as compared to ATF3 or CEBPG homodimers
source: For example, as evident from high CSI intensities, CRE-CAAT sites (red) are preferably bound by ATF3•CEBPG as compared to ATF3 or CEBPG (Figure 4C, top panel).
evidence: The results section describes preferential binding of a heterodimer to a specific site, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Scores for TRE and 5′TGACGCA3′ are higher for JUN•ATF3 than for JUN or ATF3 homodimers
source: Similarly, scores for TRE (green) and 5′TGACGCA3′ (black) are higher for JUN•ATF3 than for JUN or ATF3 (Figure 4C, middle panel).
evidence: The results section describes preferential binding of JUN•ATF3 heterodimer to specific sites, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: BATF3•ATF3 and BATF2•ATF3 enrich CRE-L sites
source: BATF3•ATF3 (Figure 4C, bottom panel) and BATF2•ATF3 (Figure 4D, top panel) enrich CRE-L sites (blue), further supporting that CRE-L is an emergent site for BATF family heterodimers (also with JUN in Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section describes CRE-L binding by BATF heterodimers, with reference to Figure 4C, 4D, and 3C.

claim: Several ATF3 heterodimers (BATF3•ATF3, JUN•ATF3, and JUNB•ATF3) can associate with the CRE site that is bound by the ATF3 homodimer
source: An important and recurring observation is that several ATF3 heterodimers (BATF3•ATF3, JUN•ATF3, and JUNB•ATF3) can associate with the CRE site that is bound by the ATF3 homodimer (Figure 4).
evidence: The results section notes that some heterodimers can bind the same sites as homodimers, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: GBM1 is an aggressive brain cancer, wherein ATF3 is a tumor suppressor and its loss of function is indicative of high-grade cancer and poor prognosis
source: The fourth cell line, GBM1 from Glioblastoma multiforme, is an aggressive brain cancer, wherein ATF3 is a tumor suppressor and its loss of function is indicative of high-grade cancer and poor prognosis (Gargiulo et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section describes the biological context of the GBM1 cell line, supported by citation.

claim: Gene ontology functional annotations of genes linked to the CRE-CAAT (blue) and TRE (green) clusters differ substantially
source: Gene ontology functional annotations of genes linked to the CRE-CAAT (blue) and TRE (green) clusters also differ substantially (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: The results section reports differences in gene ontology annotations for different clusters of ATF3-bound sites, with reference to Figure 5C and Supplementary file 1H.

claim: CRE-CAAT sites preferred by ATF3•CEBP heterodimers enriched for gene ontology terms related to immune response and JAK-STAT signaling
source: CRE-CAAT sites preferred by ATF3•CEBP heterodimers (blue cluster) enriched for gene ontology (GO) terms related to immune response and JAK-STAT signaling, whereas TRE sites (green cluster) enriched for GO terms associated to nutrient sensing, PDGF signaling, and cell junction regulation.
evidence: The results section reports specific gene ontology enrichments for different clusters of ATF3-bound sites.

claim: TRE sites enriched for GO terms associated to nutrient sensing, PDGF signaling, and cell junction regulation
source: CRE-CAAT sites preferred by ATF3•CEBP heterodimers (blue cluster) enriched for gene ontology (GO) terms related to immune response and JAK-STAT signaling, whereas TRE sites (green cluster) enriched for GO terms associated to nutrient sensing, PDGF signaling, and cell junction regulation.
evidence: The results section reports specific gene ontology enrichments for different clusters of ATF3-bound sites.

claim: Heterodimers drive cell-type and signal-specific gene networks
source: This observation lends support to the notion that heterodimers drive cell-type and signal-specific gene networks.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the gene ontology enrichment data.

claim: The locus co-occupied by ATF3 and CEBPB in H1 cells is resistant to DNAse I, suggesting that ATF3 and CEBPB are binding to a seemingly inaccessible part of the genome
source: In H1 embryonic stem cells, we identified a region on chromosome I that shows overlapping ChIP peaks for ATF3 and CEBPB (Figure 6A, top panel). This locus is also resistant to DNAse I, suggesting that ATF3 and CEBPB are binding to a seemingly inaccessible part of the genome.
evidence: The results section interprets DNase I data to infer chromatin accessibility, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: CSI-Genomescapes in the co-occupied region identified a high-intensity site for the ATF3•CEBPA heterodimer, whereas no high-intensity sequences were found for ATF3 or CEBPA homodimers
source: Plotting CSI intensities for a given TF across the genome generates CSI-Genomescapes (Figure 6A–B, bottom panels; Materials and methods). CSI-Genomescapes in the co-occupied region identified a high-intensity site for the ATF3•CEBPA heterodimer, whereas no high-intensity sequences were found for ATF3 or CEBPA homodimers (Figure 6A).
evidence: The results section describes CSI-Genomescape analysis of a co-occupied region, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The JUN•ATF3 emergent site (5′TGACGCAT3′) is within DNase I accessible euchromatin
source: Similar CSI-Genomescape analysis of a locus with overlapping ATF3 and JUN peaks readily identified the JUN•ATF3 emergent site (5′TGACGCAT3′). This site is within DNase I accessible euchromatin, and CSI-Genomescapes provide scant support for either JUN or ATF3 homodimer binding to this site (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section describes the chromatin context of the JUN•ATF3 emergent site, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: CSI-Genomescapes provide scant support for either JUN or ATF3 homodimer binding to the JUN•ATF3 emergent site
source: Similar CSI-Genomescape analysis of a locus with overlapping ATF3 and JUN peaks readily identified the JUN•ATF3 emergent site (5′TGACGCAT3′). This site is within DNase I accessible euchromatin, and CSI-Genomescapes provide scant support for either JUN or ATF3 homodimer binding to this site (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section describes CSI-Genomescape analysis showing heterodimer-specific binding, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: 1018 genomic loci are co-occupied by ATF3 and CEBPB in H1 cells
source: Next, we identified genomic loci that are co-occupied by ATF3 and CEBPB in H1 (1018 overlapping ChIP peaks) or ATF3 and JUN in K562 cells (6539 overlapping ChIP peaks; Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on co-occupied genomic loci, with reference to Figure 6C-D.

claim: 6539 genomic loci are co-occupied by ATF3 and JUN in K562 cells
source: Next, we identified genomic loci that are co-occupied by ATF3 and CEBPB in H1 (1018 overlapping ChIP peaks) or ATF3 and JUN in K562 cells (6539 overlapping ChIP peaks; Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on co-occupied genomic loci, with reference to Figure 6C-D.

claim: Regions co-occupied by ATF3 and CEBPB have higher CSI intensities when scored with ATF3•CEBP heterodimers than when scored with ATF3 and CEBP homodimers
source: Violin plots clearly demonstrate that regions co-occupied by ATF3 and CEBPB have higher CSI intensities when scored with ATF3•CEBP heterodimers than when scored with ATF3 and CEBP homodimers (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes violin plot analysis showing heterodimer-specific binding at co-occupied regions, with reference to Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: For loci co-occupied by JUN and ATF3, cognate sites for JUN•ATF3 heterodimer perform only marginally better at explaining the genomic binding data than sites preferred by JUN or ATF3 homodimers
source: In contrast, for loci co-occupied by JUN and ATF3, violin plots indicate that cognate sites for JUN•ATF3 heterodimer perform only marginally better at explaining the genomic binding data than sites preferred by JUN or ATF3 homodimers (Figure 6F, left panel).
evidence: The results section describes violin plot analysis for JUN and ATF3 co-occupied regions, with reference to Figure 6F.

claim: The perceptibly higher CSI intensity when using JUN•ATF3 cognate sites might arise from heterodimer-preferred TRE sites or heterodimer-specific emergent sites
source: This observation is consistent with the ability of the JUN•ATF3 heterodimer to bind consensus CRE sites that are also bound by each contributing homodimer. The perceptibly higher CSI intensity when using JUN•ATF3 cognate sites might arise from heterodimer-preferred TRE sites or heterodimer-specific emergent sites.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the violin plot data for JUN•ATF3.

claim: 39 co-occupied regions include emergent heterodimer-specific 5′TGACGCAT3′ sites
source: To examine this possibility, we utilized CSI-Genomescapes to score all co-occupied regions that include emergent heterodimer-specific 5′TGACGCAT3′ sites (39 sites).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data on the number of co-occupied regions containing the emergent site.

claim: When the subset of genomic regions with the emergent site was examined with homodimer CSI data, the violin plots reveal the inability of ATF3 homodimer cognate sites to account for the ChIP signals
source: When this subset of genomic regions was examined with homodimer CSI data, the violin plots reveal the inability of ATF3 homodimer cognate sites to account for the ChIP signals, whereas JUN homodimers account for some of the JUN occupancy at those regions (Figure 6F, right panel).
evidence: The results section describes violin plot analysis for regions containing the emergent site, with reference to Figure 6F.

claim: JUN homodimers account for some of the JUN occupancy at regions containing the emergent site
source: When this subset of genomic regions was examined with homodimer CSI data, the violin plots reveal the inability of ATF3 homodimer cognate sites to account for the ChIP signals, whereas JUN homodimers account for some of the JUN occupancy at those regions (Figure 6F, right panel).
evidence: The results section describes violin plot analysis for regions containing the emergent site, with reference to Figure 6F.

claim: The ATF3•JUN heterodimer cognate sites showed the highest scores for the emergent site
source: In contrast, the ATF3•JUN heterodimer cognate sites showed the highest scores for the emergent site.
evidence: The results section describes violin plot analysis showing heterodimer-specific binding to the emergent site.

claim: 5076 non-coding single-nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with diseases and quantitative traits
source: Armed with 102 CSI profiles of bZIP dimers, we scrutinized 5076 non-coding single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that are associated with diseases and quantitative traits (Maurano et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section provides the number of SNPs analyzed, supported by citation.

claim: The minor allele of rs7631605 predicts disruption of the emergent site 5′TGACGCAT3′
source: The CSI-Genomescape for rs7631605 site is particularly interesting because it predicts disruption of the emergent site 5′TGACGCAT3′ (Figure 7A middle panel).
evidence: The results section describes a prediction for how rs7631605 affects bZIP binding, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: CSI-Genomescape predicts that rs1869901 impacts binding of FOS•CEBPE by altering a TRE-CAAT site
source: Additionally, CSI-Genomescape predicts that rs1869901, a variant associated with schizophrenia, impacts binding of FOS•CEBPE by altering a TRE-CAAT site (Figure 7A bottom panel).
evidence: The results section describes a prediction for how rs1869901 affects bZIP binding, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: ChIP-seq studies in several cell lines examined by the ENCODE consortium have shown binding by FOS and JUN to rs3758354 and rs17293632 loci
source: ChIP-seq studies in several cell lines examined by the ENCODE consortium have shown binding by FOS and JUN to both loci, providing support that these sites are accessed by bZIP proteins in a cellular context (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section cites ENCODE ChIP-seq data as validation that the SNP loci are bound by bZIPs in vivo, with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: rs10994336 is predicted to increase CSI intensity by at least twofold for 44 out of 102 bZIP pairs
source: For example, rs10994336 is predicted to increase CSI intensity by at least twofold for 44 out of 102 bZIP pairs reported here.
evidence: The results section provides a specific example of a SNP with broad impact on bZIP binding.

claim: Many of the SNPs in the RegulomeDB database are annotated with PWMs derived from bZIP homodimers
source: It is particularly important to note that many of the SNPs in the database are annotated with PWMs derived from bZIP homodimers, whereas our CSI intensity fold-change predictions for 22 homo- and 80 bZIP heterodimers make use of the entire bZIP-DNA interactomes (all 10-mers).
evidence: The results section compares the current study's approach with existing SNP annotations.

claim: The ability of bZIPs to form heterodimers appears to increase with increasing evolutionary complexity
source: The ability of bZIPs to form heterodimers appears to increase with increasing evolutionary complexity, with human bZIPs displaying more intricate heterodimerization networks than C. elegans and D. melanogaster, which in turn, exhibit more complex dimerization networks than S. cerevisiae (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion describes an evolutionary trend in bZIP heterodimerization, supported by citation.

claim: Human bZIPs display more intricate heterodimerization networks than C. elegans and D. melanogaster
source: The ability of bZIPs to form heterodimers appears to increase with increasing evolutionary complexity, with human bZIPs displaying more intricate heterodimerization networks than C. elegans and D. melanogaster, which in turn, exhibit more complex dimerization networks than S. cerevisiae (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion describes comparative complexity of bZIP networks across species, supported by citation.

claim: C. elegans and D. melanogaster exhibit more complex dimerization networks than S. cerevisiae
source: The ability of bZIPs to form heterodimers appears to increase with increasing evolutionary complexity, with human bZIPs displaying more intricate heterodimerization networks than C. elegans and D. melanogaster, which in turn, exhibit more complex dimerization networks than S. cerevisiae (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion describes comparative complexity of bZIP networks across species, supported by citation.

claim: The potential for combinatorial control by bZIP heterodimers was recognized long ago
source: Given the large repertoire of human bZIP heterodimers, this family of TFs is particularly amenable to effect combinatorial control. Indeed, this potential was recognized long ago (Bohmann et al., 1987; Franza et al., 1988; Lamb and McKnight, 1991).
evidence: The discussion cites early recognition of bZIP combinatorial potential, supported by citations.

claim: An ever-increasing body of evidence now implicates bZIPs in numerous aspects of cellular and organismal function
source: An ever-increasing body of evidence now implicates bZIPs in numerous aspects of cellular and organismal function.
evidence: The discussion makes a general statement about the importance of bZIPs.

claim: bZIP dimers were under-scrutinized with only a handful of heterodimers reported prior to this work
source: However, despite large surveys charting the TF-DNA interactomes (Badis et al., 2009, 2008; Berger et al., 2008; Carlson et al., 2010; Fordyce et al., 2010; Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2014; Grove et al., 2009; Jolma et al., 2010, 2013; Kamesh et al., 2015; Nitta et al., 2015; Noyes et al., 2008; Siggers et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2010; Weirauch et al., 2014), bZIP dimers were under-scrutinized with only a handful of heterodimers reported thus far (Cohen et al., 2015; Jolma et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion contextualizes the current study within the broader field of TF-DNA interactome studies, supported by citations.

claim: It was quite unclear prior to this work how dimerization between different bZIP partners would impact DNA recognition
source: Thus, it was quite unclear prior to this work how dimerization between different bZIP partners would impact DNA recognition.
evidence: The discussion highlights the knowledge gap that this study addresses.

claim: The 270 bZIP pairs examined represent a wide survey of the 666 potential pairs that can be formed by 36 monomers
source: Guided by PPI data, we examined the DNA-binding specificities of 126 stable dimers and 144 bZIP dimers that display no dimerization even at 1 µM. These 270 bZIP pairs represent a wide survey of the 666 potential pairs that can be formed by 36 monomers.
evidence: The discussion contextualizes the scope of the study.

claim: The variably-spaced class of heterodimer binding sites comprised 12% of the sites
source: The second class contained variably-spaced half-sites, often overlapping by a single nucleotide.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the quantitative breakdown of heterodimer binding site classes (this percentage is stated in the abstract).

claim: The binding of TFs to each other, and/or to adjacent DNA sites, can influence binding specificity profiles in important ways
source: However, it is clear from our work as well as the recent work of others that the binding of TFs to each other, and/or to adjacent DNA sites, can influence binding specificity profiles in important ways (Ansari and Peterson-Kaufman, 2011; Garvie et al., 2001; Grove et al., 2009; Jolma et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2013; Siggers et al., 2012; Slattery et al., 2011).
evidence: The discussion places the current findings in the context of other studies showing the importance of protein-protein and protein-DNA interactions, supported by citations.

claim: The field will tackle the effects of higher order interactions and begin to relate these to the transcriptional control of key biological processes
source: Our study heralds the important next wave of specificity mapping, in which the field will tackle the effects of higher order interactions and begin to relate these to the transcriptional control of key biological processes.
evidence: The discussion provides a forward-looking statement about future research directions.
